description: Hi! I'm Brendan. I'm building PARALLAX, an astronaut health companion that helps a crew member answer a practical question: what do my health records actually show, what is still missing, and what should I do next?
summary:
PARALLAX: Health beyond Earth. PARALLAX is an astronaut health monitoring companion that helps a crew member answer a practical question: what do my health records actually show, what is still missing, and what should I do next?

Our demonstration follows Alex Morgan, a fictional astronaut the day before a Mars landing. PARALLAX brings preflight baselines and in-flight observations together. It compares them only when the measurement conditions match, names the information that is still missing and guides the astronaut to retrieve it. During simulated wearable monitoring, the heart rate stays at 72 bpm but the sensor reports a disconnection. PARALLAX withholds that reading and sends an event that a separate crew companion acknowledges. Each cycle ends in a saved human review with a structured handoff and a list of next health actions, so the next assessment starts from what is still unknown.

The design draws on the NASA Human Research Program and the NASA-STD-3001 human-performance standards, and the app runs locally and offline in the browser. It is a working prototype that uses fictional data. It does not diagnose.
details:
PARALLAX AT A GLANCE

- What it is: a working, browser-based astronaut health monitoring companion. It helps a crew member understand what their health observations actually show, what is still missing, and what to do next.

- Challenge: 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.

- Who it is for: astronauts reviewing their own health on long-duration missions, with a qualified crew medical officer or flight surgeon reviewing the record afterwards.

- Core idea: having a measurement does not necessarily mean it answers the health question that matters.

- Key features: acquisition-aware comparisons, missing-information guidance with retrieval, signal-quality-aware heart-rate monitoring, a crew companion for event acknowledgment, a saved human review with HTML and JSON handoff, a post-review health action plan, and offline operation.

- NASA resources used: the NASA Human Research Program (hazards and risks), the NASA-STD-3001 Human-Systems Standards (4.0 Human Performance, 6.0 Medical Operations), the Human Research Roadmap sensorimotor gap SM-204, NASA exercise and CEVIS resources, NASA technical reports, and NASA-associated ISS and bed-rest study data.

- Space agency partner: the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Bio-Monitor, as wearable-monitoring context.

- Status: working prototype using fictional astronaut data. IIts base build passes 511 automated unit and scenario tests and 211 automated browser workflows. It is not clinically validated and does not diagnose.

- Try it: https://parallax-health.brendanlimkh04.workers.dev/

TOMORROW, YOU LAND ON MARS.

Alex Morgan has spent nearly six months in microgravity aboard Aster, a fictional crewed mission to Mars. The crew lands tomorrow, and every message to Earth now takes minutes each way.

Alex has plenty of health data: preflight reference tests, cycle-ergometer exercise sessions, gas-analysis oxygen-uptake measurements, a sleep diary and a wearable heart-rate monitor. What Alex lacks is a clear answer to a simpler question. What do these records actually tell me, what is still missing, and what should I do next?

PARALLAX answers that question. It organises scattered observations into understandable findings, names the missing information and shows how to obtain it, checks whether a monitored signal is still usable, and keeps everything in a human review that the crew can save and hand off. Our tagline is Health beyond Earth.

THE CHALLENGE WE ADDRESS

The challenge asks for software that "gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health", because on long missions astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in themselves.

Three problems make that self-assessment hard, and each one grows as a mission travels farther from Earth:

1. Measurements are taken under different conditions. A heart rate recorded on Earth at 100 W, an in-flight heart rate at the same workload and a wearable reading with unknown activity can all be subtracted from one another. Only some of those subtractions mean anything.

2. Important information is often missing. A screen full of numbers can hide the question that nobody can answer yet.

3. Sensors fail quietly. A heart-rate number can stay on screen after the sensor has lost contact.

AN ASTRONAUT'S JOURNEY: WHAT PARALLAX DOES

The guided demonstration uses the application's real controls and state. All individual measurements are fictional.

1. Preflight: personal baselines. Alex's Earth baselines are 1,000 N leg-press force, a measured absolute VO₂peak of 3.0 L/min, an exercise heart rate of 120 bpm at 100 W and 7.5 hours of reported sleep. Each baseline keeps its acquisition context: Earth, 1 g, equipment and protocol. PARALLAX does not assume that the Earth context matches later in-flight conditions.

2. Transit: recorded changes over time. Compatible in-flight pairs show a measured VO₂peak of 2.8 → 2.7 L/min and reported sleep of 7.5 → 6.5 hours. Two cycling sessions at 100 W record 125 and 140 bpm. The later record sits in a fictional onboard archive, outside the active review. PARALLAX presents these as descriptive changes, not diagnoses.

3. Approach: find what is missing. The day before landing, the health review has evidence for 2 of 3 named information requirements. PARALLAX identifies the missing exercise record. Alex inspects it in the archive, confirms its conditions match (100 W, final minute of the session) and adds it to the review. The comparison now shows +15 bpm at the same workload, and information coverage moves from 2/3 to 3/3. This counts information, not medical or landing readiness. Current muscular strength and post-landing mobility remain visibly unresolved.

4. Monitoring: when 72 bpm stops being usable evidence. PARALLAX demonstrates two separate simulated equipment sources:

- synthetic wearable heart-rate and signal-quality data in the documented commercial Astroskin format, with the CSA Bio-Monitor as spaceflight context;

- PARALLAX-defined fictional stored exercise records, inspired by NASA's CEVIS cycle ergometer.

The app does not connect to either device yet. In the wearable replay, a raw heart rate of 72 bpm is usable under the demonstration policy. One second later the number is still 72 bpm, but the source's quality mask reports a garment disconnection. PARALLAX withholds the current observation, marks the gap on the chart and records a persistent quality event. A separate companion browser tab receives the event, Alex acknowledges it, and the original tab records the acknowledgment.

The number stayed the same. Its reliability changed. A disconnection is a data-quality event. It is not a physiological emergency, and a restored signal does not mean recovery.

5. Human review. A fictional crew medical officer reviews every current finding, the evidence limitations, the unresolved requirements, the monitoring facts, the event and its acknowledgment. The officer selects a disposition and reasons and saves the review. PARALLAX produces a human-readable HTML review and a structured JSON handoff from the same saved snapshot. It never generates a medical clearance.

6. Surface: the cycle continues. After the review is saved, PARALLAX shows "Your next health actions": plan the surface mobility assessment, review strength requirements against the historical 1,000 N preflight reference, and follow up monitoring events. This status is kept separate from the saved review, which never changes, so the next assessment cycle starts from what is still unknown. A planning request is recorded locally, for qualified review; it is not scheduling, transmission or a completed assessment. Earlier observations cannot establish walking or balance at 0.38 g, so they stay labelled as historical.

WHAT MAKES PARALLAX DIFFERENT

- Acquisition-aware comparisons. A difference appears only when the measurement identity and the recorded conditions support it. A mathematically correct difference is not always a meaningful comparison.

- Evidence-aware next steps. The recommendations are concrete information actions (retrieve this record, inspect this source, designate this monitoring requirement), not vague health advice.

- Signal-quality-aware monitoring. The same raw number can be usable evidence or a withheld observation, depending on what the source reports about its quality.

- Human-centred review. Software organises the evidence, and a person makes the decision. The review records both and keeps them separate.

- Local operation. After the first load, the core workflows run in the browser without a server or an internet connection. This matters for missions with long communication delays.

HOW NASA RESOURCES SHAPED PARALLAX

NASA resources decide what PARALLAX asks and what it refuses to claim. Each one maps to a feature:

- NASA Human Research Program, Five Hazards and Hazard: Distance From Earth. Frame the problem; motivate local, offline operation and a structured handoff.

- NASA Human Research Program, Risks of Human Spaceflight; NASA Aerobic and Sensorimotor Risk pages. Define separate cardiovascular, aerobic, musculoskeletal and sensorimotor health domains in the review.

- NASA-STD-3001, 4.0 Human Performance. Separates aerobic capacity, sensorimotor function and muscle strength. This is why VO₂peak, exercise heart rate, force and mobility are never substituted for each other, and why strength and mobility stay unresolved at 3/3 coverage.

- NASA-STD-3001, 6.0 Medical Operations and 3.0 Health and Medical Care; NASA OCHMO In-Flight Medical Care. Place medical judgment with qualified personnel. This is why PARALLAX ends in a human review and never issues a clearance or treatment.

- NASA Human Research Roadmap gap SM-204 (post-landing self-testing); NASA crew egress risk. Explain why post-landing mobility is a named open requirement in the Surface chapter.

- NASA Astronaut Exercise (CEVIS), OCHMO-TB-031 Exercise Overview, JSC Exercise Countermeasures. Define the exercise acquisition context: workload in watts and final-minute heart rate.

- NASA NTRS 20140003747 (in-flight oxygen uptake). Keeps VO₂peak as a separate gas-analysis measurement, never estimated from heart rate.

- NASA Standard Measures, NASA sleep-loss risk and the Fatigue Countermeasures Laboratory. Keep reported sleep as its own self-reported domain, with no fatigue diagnosis.

- NASA Ames Earth-independent medical operations work and NTRS 20220017856. Support the case for local review and a structured handoff on deep-space missions.

- NASA-associated ISS and bed-rest study data (Mulavara et al., 2018; NASA 70-day bed rest, Cromwell et al., 2018). Attributed group values appear on the Research page. They show that strength and functional performance can change differently.

PARALLAX uses no NASA participant-level data yet, and no NASA endorsement is implied. All links are listed in the NASA Data section.

WORKED RESEARCH EXAMPLE: THE SAME RULE ON PUBLISHED DATA

On its Research page, PARALLAX applies the same rule to published data. Clément et al. (2024, CC BY 4.0) report tandem-walking performance before and after 30 days of head-down-tilt bed rest. For the Exercise group, eyes-closed performance fell from 83.9% to 62.6% (−21.3 percentage points), and eyes-open performance fell from 98.5% to 87.9% (−10.6 points). If the eyes-closed baseline is paired with the eyes-open follow-up, the arithmetic gives an apparent improvement of +4.0 points. PARALLAX shows this only as misleading arithmetic and withholds the comparison, because the conditions differ. These are published group means from a ground study. They are not individual astronaut data and do not validate PARALLAX clinically.

HOW IT WORKS (TECHNOLOGY)

PARALLAX is a static single-page web application written in TypeScript with React. It uses no server, no user accounts and no AI model at runtime.

- Observation register and comparison engine. Every record carries typed acquisition declarations (gravity, equipment, workload, timing, protocol and origin). A change is calculated only for compatible records. Otherwise it is withheld with a reason.

- Requirements model. Each review has named information items. Coverage counts only those items, and historical evidence stays separate.

- Documented-format adapter. Parses heart-rate (datatype 19) and signal-quality (datatype 1000) frames as described in the public Astroskin API documentation, and aligns quality to each sample by exact time.

- Event ledger and crew companion. Events, receipts and acknowledgments are stored in IndexedDB. A companion tab in the same browser receives them through BroadcastChannel, with durable reconciliation.

- Saved reviews and offline use. Saved reviews do not change, and later evidence marks them as outdated. A service worker supports offline use after the first load.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Vite, Vitest, Playwright, axe-core, ESLint, Prettier and Lucide icons. No special hardware is required.

WHAT HAS BEEN DEMONSTRATED

The live release (PARALLAX 0.10.0-alpha.10, release guide-hotfix.1) is the base build e53055a plus a compact layout fix to the guide panel. The base build passes 511 automated unit and scenario tests and 211 automated Chromium browser workflows, with zero skipped or flaky results. The guide fix changed only the guide's display code. For the live release we re-ran 36 relevant unit tests, 8 browser regressions and the full guided and short judging journeys through the application's real controls, including the separate companion acknowledgment, the saved review and use offline after installation. All passed. The full 511/211 suite was not repeated on the fix, and the live /evaluation.txt states this. The full production build is only about 1.5 MB.

These results are automated software verification. They are not clinical validation or a human usability study. No astronauts, clinicians or other evaluators have tested PARALLAX (N = 0).

HOW PARALLAX ADDRESSES THE JUDGING CRITERIA

- Impact: crews on Mars-class missions will review more of their own health with delayed ground support. PARALLAX makes that information better organised, more understandable and more trustworthy. The same pattern applies to analog missions and remote stations.

- Creativity: instead of another dashboard, PARALLAX treats the conditions of a measurement, the missing information and the quality of a signal as first-class findings. Its signature example is the same 72 bpm reading being usable one second and withheld the next.

- Validity: every claim is bounded by its source. The software is working, tested and usable through a guided demonstration, and its limitations are stated next to the features they govern.

- Relevance: it directly addresses the challenge. It gathers health indicators, charts changes over time, prompts concrete actions and explains measurements and risks. NASA Human Research Program and Human-Systems Standards resources shape the core logic (see above).

- Presentation: one astronaut, one mission and one memorable moment, shown with real screenshots in a seven-slide demo and a guided in-app walkthrough.

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE DEVELOPMENT

PARALLAX is a prototype that uses fictional data. It does not diagnose conditions, prescribe treatment, triage, or determine landing or EVA readiness. It does not connect to physical hardware and does not implement an official CEVIS data protocol. Where the challenge mentions treatment guidance, PARALLAX deliberately stops at information-handling actions and leaves treatment to qualified medical workflows.

Next steps:

- integrate physical equipment through validated interfaces;

- integrate the review handoff with qualified medical workflows;

- run human-factors evaluation with astronauts, analog crews and clinicians;

- carry out clinical and mission-specific validation.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

PARALLAX was built with substantial help from SI tools (ChatGPT, OpenAI Codex and Claude Code). They were used for research, concept refinement, design, most of the application code and tests, the fictional data and synthetic heart-rate frames, documentation and this submission. The application itself runs no AI model and sends no data to any AI service. SI-generated images carry a visible "SI-assisted" or "AI-assisted illustration" label. Product screenshots are real captures of the app. No SI-generated content uses NASA branding.

EXPERIENCE PARALLAX

- Application: https://parallax-health.brendanlimkh04.workers.dev/

- Full guided demonstration: https://parallax-health.brendanlimkh04.workers.dev/?demo=full#mission/preflight

- Short judging path: https://parallax-health.brendanlimkh04.workers.dev/?demo=short#mission/health

- Seven-slide demo: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1isi_zfak3C9-SDF24YoQM0p5lqMnwCom?usp=sharing

For the best experience, use a current desktop version of Chrome or Edge. The companion step opens a second tab in the same browser.

NASA Imagery and Attribution

PARALLAX incorporates publicly available NASA photographs to illustrate real astronaut exercise, physiological monitoring and human spaceflight research.

  • CEVIS exercise aboard the International Space Station — NASA / Johnson Space Center, image iss070e070028.
  • Spinal ultrasound investigation — NASA, image ISS036-E-035750.
  • VO₂max exercise investigation using CEVIS — NASA / Johnson Space Center, image iss030e132542.

Sources:

  • https://www.nasa.gov/general/astronaut-exercise/

These photographs are used for educational and informational purposes. Images have been resized and compressed for web delivery.

PARALLAX is an independent hackathon prototype. No NASA or astronaut endorsement, affiliation, participation or clinical validation is implied.
